strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in clinical ML by combining domain adaptation with concept-grounded interpretability, a timely and practically relevant contribution
Solid technical approach with theoretical support: Lemma 1 and Proposition 1 rigorously establish properties of M-orthogonal projection and decomposition optimality
Comprehensive experimental validation across two large real-world EHR datasets (eICU: 9.4K patients, OCHIN: 199.7K patients) with multiple domain partition settings (spatial, temporal, facility-type)

Strong empirical results with consistent 9-16% relative F1 improvements across tasks, thorough ablation studies (Table 2) demonstrating necessity of components, and linear probe analysis (Table 3) validating factorization quality

Practical interpretability demonstration via four-quadrant categorization (Figure 2, Appendix J) that distinguishes transferable predictive evidence from shift-sensitive factors with clinically plausible examples
Excellent presentation quality with clear writing, comprehensive appendices (25+ pages), detailed implementation guidance (Appendix I.2), and extensive supplementary analyses
weaknesses: Informal theoretical justification for domain separation: the core claim that orthogonality encourages domain information into z (Section 3.4 Remark) uses informal notation and unstated assumptions rather than formal theorems; lacks rigorous characterization of when/why the decomposition succeeds

Insufficient clinical validation of interpretability: claims rest entirely on qualitative case studies of 2 patients with no clinician feedback, structured evaluation, or comparison to clinician-understood baselines (attention, rule-based methods); assessment of 'clinical plausibility' by authors only, not independent domain experts

Arbitrary design choices lack principled justification: SAE latent dimension (k=2d) chosen without sensitivity analysis; interpretation thresholds (Δprob=0.05, rank-based domain sensitivity) appear pragmatic rather than principled; three-stage training lacks ablation on joint vs. staged optimization; limited hyperparameter sensitivity analysis

Unexplored accuracy-interpretability tradeoff: paper claims achieving both without analyzing conflicts; missing ablations on interpretability overhead; no comparison to interpretable-only baselines to quantify value of orthogonal decomposition

Severe performance degradation under realistic facility-type shifts (Section 4.6): Mental Health and SBHC facilities show 20% performance drops even with ExtraCare, suggesting orthogonal decomposition may not handle hardest domain gaps effectively
Multi-stage training complexity (epochs 1-10 vs. 11-30) lacks ablation on stage ordering, duration, and joint optimization; raises deployment brittleness concerns

Baseline fairness concerns: RSDA and RCG have self-training removed 'for fair comparison', making comparison less representative; missing domain generalization method comparisons; temporal shift experiments conflate diagnostic practice evolution with distribution shift

Limited scope: assumes unlabeled target data available (semi-supervised) without sensitivity analysis; only covariate shift considered, not label shift; method-specific to Transformer backbones; both datasets from US healthcare only

strengths: Well-motivated problem: addresses genuine gap between existing DA methods and clinical trustworthiness requirements
Comprehensive experimental setup: two large-scale EHR datasets (eICU, OCHIN) with multiple domain partition settings and careful preprocessing
Solid technical execution: mathematical framework with rigorous treatment of M-induced geometry (Lemma 1, Proposition 1) and detailed appendices
Thorough empirical evaluation: multiple baselines, ablation studies (Table 2), and facility-type analysis (Section 4.6) showing consistent improvements
Practical case studies: Figure 2 and Appendix J provide clinically plausible sparse dimension interpretations with four-quadrant categorization
Clear presentation: well-organized notation, algorithm pseudocode, and comprehensive implementation details facilitate reproducibility
weaknesses: Incomplete theoretical justification: Core claim that orthogonal decomposition separates label/domain information lacks rigorous proof. Remark uses informal inequalities (≳, ≲) without universal validity. Proposition 1 establishes geometric orthogonality but not information separation.

Contradiction in validation: Table 3 shows cosine similarity 0.49-0.75 between class classifier on v and v₀, contradicting claims that domain info is cleanly moved to z. This undermines the core decomposition argument.

Insufficient interpretation evaluation: No quantitative metrics for explanation quality. No clinician validation studies. Domain sensitivity defined arbitrarily as top-5 vs. bottom-5 by rank without justification. Case studies limited to 2 patients.
Modest empirical improvements: 1-3% gains on most metrics (Table 2). Ablation shows w/o M,z⊥p causes only 0.2-1.4% degradation, questioning necessity of dictionary-induced orthogonality.

Experimental design issues: (1) Spatial split selects region with largest gap (selection bias), (2) Temporal split creates class imbalance (test set larger than train: 120,917 vs 78,786), (3) Some baselines (RCG, CST) dropped for diagnosis task due to incompatibility.

Incremental technical novelty: Combines existing techniques (MMD alignment from Long et al. 2015; SAE from AutoCodeDL 2024; orthogonal decomposition from DSN 2016). Each component individually known; combination is reasonable but incremental.
Three-stage training unjustified: Sequential optimization of L_label, then L_rec, then L_dcl can be suboptimal. No justification provided; no ablation comparing to joint optimization.
Interpretation methodology borrowed: SAE-based interpretation and sparse dimension ablation directly adopted from AutoCodeDL (Wu et al., 2024) without significant innovation.
Missing statistical rigor: Standard errors often <0.3% but no significance tests. No confidence intervals. Multiple comparisons without correction.
Inadequate ethics discussion: Clinical AI system with brief dismissive impact statement. No discussion of failure modes, fairness, or potential harms.

strengths: Novel technical approach combining SAE-driven sparse features with M-orthogonal decomposition for interpretable domain adaptation; Proposition 1 and Lemma 1 provide solid theoretical grounding for closed-form projection and stability

Strong empirical results showing 12-16% relative F1 improvements over baselines across multiple domain partition settings (spatial, temporal, facility-specific) on two large-scale EHR datasets with proper ablations
Comprehensive experimental design including >10 baselines (DANN, RMMD, RSDA, BUA, DAL, RCG, CST, SSRT), oracle/base bounds, and systematic ablation studies demonstrating each component's necessity

Practical interpretability innovation via four-quadrant categorization (label impact × domain sensitivity) that maps sparse dimensions to ICD codes and distinguishes transferable from shift-sensitive evidence

Excellent reproducibility with detailed implementation (Appendix I.2), hyperparameters, data splits, comprehensive notation table, and algorithm pseudocode; clinical deployment considerations discussed
Addresses genuine gap in clinical DA—combines robustness (accuracy) with transparency (interpretability), filling important need in healthcare where explainability is prerequisite for adoption
Linear probe analysis (Table 3) provides quantitative evidence of effective feature disentanglement across multiple tasks
weaknesses: Interpretability validation is primarily qualitative—case studies (Figure 2, Appendix J.2-J.4) are illustrative but anecdotal; lacks quantitative metrics, inter-rater reliability studies, or user validation with clinicians to demonstrate explanations are actually useful or trustworthy

Theoretical justification for domain concentration in z relies on informal information-theoretic bounds (≳, ≲ relations) rather than rigorous guarantees; no empirical validation that z independently captures domain information (Table 3 shows 0.09 cosine similarity Wc(v0) vs Wc(z), indicating residual label information)
Limited scope evaluated only on EHR diagnosis and heart failure prediction; generalization to other medical domains (imaging, genomics), prediction tasks, or non-US healthcare systems remains unclear

Model complexity with multiple interacting components (MMD alignment, SAE reconstruction, orthogonal projection, domain classification) and numerous hyperparameters (λ1, λ2, λ3, ε)—limited sensitivity analysis or justification for design choices (e.g., why latent dimension 256=2d?)

Domain sensitivity annotation uses ad-hoc rank-based criterion (top-5/bottom-5) rather than principled thresholding; ∆prob=0.05 threshold for label impact appears arbitrary without systematic justification

Baseline modifications (removing self-training from RSDA/RCG, incompatibility of RCG/CST with multi-label diagnosis) raise fair comparison concerns; some improvements within ±1-2 standard errors of baselines
Three-stage training schedule lacks justification—why not joint optimization? The stopped-gradient operation on v_μ in Eq. (3) unexplained; no ablation on whether staged training is necessary

Dataset characteristics limit claims: OCHIN temporal split heavily imbalanced (2012-2021 vs 2022-2023); Figure 3 facility-based evaluation shows substantial performance degradation under severe shifts

Missing practical considerations: no computational cost analysis, failure mode discussion, or analysis of how results degrade under extreme shifts; limited discussion of when domain adaptation should NOT be used

Ethical/fairness analysis under-discussed: no investigation whether domain shifts reflect clinically meaningful differences vs artifacts, no bias analysis across patient subgroups, limited discussion of potential harms from misinterpreting domain-sensitive signals

strengths: Novel and well-motivated combination of sparse autoencoders with orthogonal inference for transparent domain adaptation in clinical settings, addressing an important gap where most DA methods lack interpretability
Comprehensive experimental validation across spatial and temporal domain shifts on two large real-world EHR datasets (eICU, OCHIN) with consistent improvements (12-16% F1 gains)
Strong interpretability validation (RQ3) with external grounding metrics (LAD, DAD, QCE) and both LLM (68%) and human (64%) preference validation, providing compelling evidence beyond model internals

Clinically useful four-quadrant categorization framework (high/low label impact × high/low domain sensitivity) that enables clinicians to distinguish transferable evidence from shift-sensitive variation
Rigorous mathematical framework with formally proven theoretical results (Lemma 1 on stability, Proposition 1 on closed-form solution) and proper treatment of the dictionary-induced metric
Thorough reproducibility documentation including detailed implementation (Section I.2), pseudocode, hyperparameters, and extensive appendices with ablations and sensitivity analyses

Comprehensive baseline comparisons (10+ methods) including recent clinical DA work, ablation studies demonstrating contribution of each component, and functional validation through residual masking intervention
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—primarily combines existing techniques (SAE from AutoCodeDL, orthogonal decomposition from Domain Separation Networks); the contribution is in their combination rather than fundamental innovation

Critical design choices lack justification: three-stage training procedure never ablated against joint training; SAE latent dimension k=2d relegated to appendix without justification or sensitivity analysis; stopped-gradient in Eq. 3 unexplained; sparse dimension selection (top-3) appears arbitrary

Interpretability evaluation of RQ2 predominantly qualitative with only 2 patients shown; ∆prob=0.05 threshold seems arbitrary despite robustness analysis in Appendix K.2; domain sensitivity uses rank-based rather than magnitude-based annotation without justification

Mathematical exposition issues: Definition 1 introduced formally before intuition; Remark on domain information uses informal relations (≳, ≲) acknowledged as 'not strict or universally valid'; information-theoretic argument in Appendix D lacks rigor with unspecified regularity conditions

Minimal ethics engagement for a healthcare paper: Impact statement claims nothing needs highlighting; no discussion of fairness across patient subgroups, privacy concerns, data biases, or prospective clinical validation requirements

Limited experimental scope: only two US-based datasets (both diagnosis-focused); domain generalization methods missing as baselines; no statistical significance testing; domain partition choices appear arbitrary (why West/Midwest vs Northeast/South?)

Several ablation results suggest limited contribution of some components: w/o L_dcl shows only 0.5-2% F1 drop, questioning necessity of explicit domain classification; w/o L_rec & L_dcl shows modest degradation, raising questions about component interactions

Reproducibility gaps: no code release; many hyperparameters with sensitivity analysis only for ∆prob threshold; scalability implications of SAE training not discussed; unclear how method extends to >2 domains; hyperparameter tuning burden not addressed

strengths: Addresses an important and well-motivated problem: domain shift in clinical prediction with emphasis on transparency in high-stakes settings
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with two real-world EHR datasets (eICU, OCHIN), multiple domain shift scenarios, and extensive baselines (8+ comparison methods)
Thoughtful approach to external validation of explanations (RQ3) using patient relevance and facility specificity anchors grounded in clinical data
Positive empirical results with improvements over strong baselines across multiple tasks and datasets
Extensive supplementary materials with detailed implementation, ablations, and interpretation protocols support potential reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines existing components (SAEs from AutoCodeDL, orthogonal decomposition from prior works like Domain Separation Networks and RCG) without introducing fundamentally new insights into domain adaptation or interpretability

Weak justification for the orthogonal inference design: (1) Why is the reconstruction direction v̂ the right reference for domain/label separation? (2) Why measure reconstruction error under the dictionary-induced metric M rather than standard Euclidean norm? (3) The theoretical propositions/lemmas are standard linear algebra without novel insights

Questionable experimental fairness: ExtraCare uses 3 training stages and 3 loss terms while most baselines use 1-2 objectives, giving ExtraCare significantly more optimization flexibility; this advantage should be controlled for with equivalent baseline versions

Interpretation validation relies on arbitrary design choices: ∆prob = 0.05 threshold for label impact is not principled; domain sensitivity uses coarse rank-based criterion (top-5/bottom-5); external grounding improvements are modest (LAD 36→47%, DAD 40→42%, QCE 37→32%); human preference only 68% vs SAE baseline

Weak theoretical contribution: No formal analysis of what orthogonal decomposition achieves for domain adaptation; does not apply Ben-David domain adaptation theory; no theoretical bound relating orthogonality to target generalization; the information-theoretic remark uses informal notation and acknowledged non-strict bounds

Missing or incomplete ablations: no sensitivity analysis for SAE hyperparameters/initialization; sparse dimension size (k=2d) choice unjustified; multi-stage training schedule sensitivity unexplored; unclear how much improvement comes from SAE vs orthogonal decomposition individually; Table 4 shows conflicting evidence (v maintains high label information while being aligned across domains)

Limited clinical validation: external grounding through prevalence is not true clinical validation; no user studies with clinicians on actionability of explanations; four-quadrant categorization utility not validated; limited to diagnosis/HF prediction on specific datasets

Dense presentation that obscures key insights: the connection between reconstruction-based orthogonality and domain/label separation is not intuitive; multiple hyperparameters (λ₁, λ₂, λ₃, γ, ε) make it difficult to understand what drives improvements; some improvements fall within reported standard error ranges without significance testing

strengths: Addresses critical gap in clinical ML: Making domain adaptation transparent and interpretable for high-stakes deployment is important and underexplored
Technically sound methodology: Dictionary-induced metric M is well-motivated; Lemma 1 and Proposition 1 provide theoretical grounding for orthogonal decomposition

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Two complementary real-world EHR datasets, multiple realistic domain shifts (spatial, temporal, facility-type), consistent improvements (9-16% relative F1 gains), thorough ablations demonstrating each component's contribution

Novel interpretability framework: Four-quadrant categorization (label impact × domain sensitivity) is intuitive and clinically actionable; external grounding protocol (RQ3) with LAD/DAD/QCE metrics rigorously validates explanations against independent anchors
Practical relevance: Facility-type adaptation (Section 4.7) demonstrates robustness under realistic shifts; interpretability enables clinician auditing rather than black-box optimization
Rigorous presentation and reproducibility: Formal mathematical exposition, extensive appendices with proofs and details, pseudocode, hyperparameters, and dataset statistics support reproducibility

Strong experimental rigor: Fair baseline comparisons, proper train/val/test splits, ablation studies convincingly demonstrate design choices, qualitative case studies (J.2) support interpretability claims
weaknesses: Theoretical gaps: Remark on 'Domain Information in z' uses informal relations (≳, ≲) with unspecified conditions rather than rigorous bounds; connection between alignment in v-space and reduced I(δ; v) lacks formal proof; weakens theoretical contribution
Limited technical novelty: Core components (SAE, orthogonal decomposition) exist in prior work; primary novelty is combining with dictionary-induced metric M, which feels somewhat incremental

Interpretation evaluation limitations: External anchors are heuristic (simple membership check for relevance); domain sensitivity uses arbitrary rank-based thresholds; human evaluation small (25 cases from 2 experts); Table 10 shows non-negligible sensitivity to label-impact threshold τ; no clinical expert validation of whether four-quadrant framework improves decision-making

Scope limited to code-level prediction: Interpretation pipeline specifically leverages ICD code structure via ablation; inapplicable to general EHR prediction (mortality, length-of-stay, lab values); narrower applicability than suggested
Modest empirical improvements: 12% relative gain on eICU diagnosis solid but not dramatic; 9% on HF trails best baseline; large gap to Oracle remains; interpretability is primary contribution

Domain classification design underexplored: Unlike standard disentanglement work, explicitly supervises z for domain classification; justified through informal information-theoretic argument but limited empirical comparison (ablation 'w/o Ldcl' insufficient)

Hyperparameter sensitivity underexplored: Introduces λ₁, λ₂, λ₃, γ, ε with limited sensitivity analysis; ε's stabilization role mathematically important but practically treated as constant; two-stage training schedule appears critical but lacks justification

Incomplete failure mode analysis: No discussion of when domain and label information are entangled; Figure 4 shows larger degradation in Mental Health/SBHC but limited analysis of why; missing adversarial examples
Limited evaluation scope: Only two prediction tasks on two similar datasets (both ICD code-based); no evaluation on non-code prediction or multimodal data; US EHR system focus limits generalization

Minimal clinical deployment discussion: Perfunctory impact statement; no fairness analysis across subgroups (age, gender, race, comorbidities); no discussion of unclear four-quadrant categorization cases; risk mitigation strategies missing
